name: tutorial_lobbying_triage
document:
# Tutorial: Lobbying Say-versus-Do (deliberately artificial sample)

## Purpose

A lobbying filing says what an organisation paid to ask government for. A public
commitment says what that same organisation told everyone else it would do. Reporting in
this genre is almost always the join of the two: the lead is not a filing on its own, it
is a filing that asks for the opposite of what its client promised in public. This
tutorial workflow reads each filing, joins it to its client's public commitment, asks a
model which pairs contradict, and publishes the contradictions a person has reviewed.

The sample data is INVENTED. Every organisation is fictional, nothing is fetched from the
network, and no row describes a real filing, client, firm or commitment.

## Input data

Two bundled CSVs.

`tutorial_lobbying_triage.csv`, one row per filing:

- `filing_id` — stable, unique identifier for the filing
- `client` — the organisation that retained the lobbyists
- `registrant` — the lobbying firm that filed the disclosure
- `amount_usd` — reported lobbying spend for the period, as the filing writes it, e.g. "$185,000"
- `filing_period` — the reporting period, e.g. "2024 Q1"
- `specific_issues` — the filer's own one-line account of what this filing asked for

`tutorial_public_commitments.csv`, one row per organisation:

- `client` — the organisation that made the commitment
- `public_commitment` — one line of what it said in public it would do
- `commitment_source` — where it said it, e.g. "2023 climate pledge"

## Step 1 — Check every filing before anything reads it

Read each filing's reported spend out of the text the filing writes it in — "$185,000"
becomes 185000 — so that every later step is weighing a number rather than a string that
looks like one. A filing whose spend cannot be read is not carried forward with a blank
in its place: the run stops and says which filing it was. The same goes for a filing that
says nothing about what it asked government for, because there is no ask to judge. This
is plain code, not the model: reading a dollar figure has one right answer.

## Step 2 — Join each filing to its client's public commitment

Bring `public_commitment` and `commitment_source` onto every filing, matched on
the client name. This is a many-to-one join: the commitments file carries at most one row
per organisation, and a repeat would fail the run rather than quietly multiply filings.
No filing is dropped here. A filing whose client has no commitment row keeps every one of
its own fields and carries a blank commitment — the absence is the record, and the next
step is told to read it as an absence rather than as a judgment.

## Step 3 — Judge the filing against the commitment (LLM)

For each filing, read the client's public commitment and this filing's ask together, and
add two fields — one filing in, one filing out (the filing is neither dropped nor duplicated):

- `alignment` — one of: Contradicts, Matches, Unclear, No commitment given. "Contradicts"
  means this filing asks government for the opposite of what the client committed to.
  "No commitment given" is the answer when the commitment field is blank. Every filing
  gets one of the four and none is left blank: the absent-commitment case already has its
  own label, so a blank would be a hole in what the report later prints rather than an
  answer.
- `alignment_note` — a single plain sentence naming what the client said and what this
  filing asks for.

The model is given only these two texts, and is told not to use anything it knows about
the organisation and not to invent a commitment that is not in front of it. The step
names the model it runs on, so the run records which model answered rather than whichever
one the platform happened to default to that week.

Filings are read up to twelve at a time in one model call — up to, because the last call
of a run holds whatever is left over. This is a cost trade: one call carrying twelve
filings is far cheaper than twelve calls carrying one. What it costs is independence,
since the filings sharing a call are judged beside each other, so a filing's answer could
be swayed by the ones it happens to travel with.

## Step 4 — Put every contradiction in front of a person

A contradiction is the one judgment this workflow publishes as a finding, so the model's
is not the one that gets published. Every filing the model called "Contradicts" is queued
for a human, largest reported spend first, and the run stops there — nothing below this
step runs until each queued filing has been decided.

The reviewer is shown the filing, the ask as filed, the commitment as said and the model's
label, and records a label of their own in `reviewed_alignment`. The model's `alignment` is
left exactly as the model wrote it, so what the model said and what the person decided are
both on the record afterwards. Beside their label the reviewer records the name they
reviewed under, the moment they decided, and a note naming the words in the two texts they
decided from.

This step decides nothing itself. A queued filing with no recorded decision stays queued
and the run stays stopped: there is no wait that expires and no label that stands in for
one nobody chose. A filing the model did not call a contradiction is not queued, is read
by nobody, and passes through unchanged.

After this step every filing carries `review_verdict`: "approve" where the reviewer kept
the model's label, "modify" where they changed it, and "skipped" for a filing no person
was asked about — so a judgment a person reviewed can be told from one only the model made.

## Step 5 — Publish the report

Produce a single HTML page listing every filing with client, registrant,
reported spend, what the filing asked for, what the client committed to in public (or that
no commitment is on record), and the judgment as it stands after review. The label the page
prints is the reviewer's, not the model's: a filing whose reviewer changed the label is no
longer printed as a contradiction, and a contradiction they confirmed carries their name,
the time they reviewed it and the note they left. A filing shown as a contradiction also
shows both sides side by side — the commitment as said, and the ask as filed — so the page
carries the contradiction itself rather than a bare label. A judgment recorded as reviewed
with nobody's name against it is not published at all: the step stops instead. No score, no
ranking and no recommendation: the report is a reading aid, not a verdict.

Every row also carries a link back to that row's lineage — each stage that touched it, back
to the input row it came from — so a reader can check any line of the page against the run.

The page's markup and stylesheet live in the step that writes them, so a reviewer reads
the markup and the code that fills it together.

## Out of scope

No external fetching, no filing dropped anywhere, and no second join — one check, one
join, one model read, one human review, one page.

stages.description: Join Each Filing to its Client's Public Commitment
compiler_notes: enrich, not expand: the commitments file is one row per organisation, so a repeated client is a data error the runtime should fail the run on rather than silently multiplying filings.

A LEFT join, so no filing is dropped. A filing whose client has no commitment row survives carrying nulls in both landed columns, and its ABSENT second parent is what the run's lineage view shows — a null here means 'no row matched', which the next step reads as an absence rather than as a judgment.
`client` is the join key on both sides and needs no enrich_with entry; the two landed columns are named the same on both sides because the subject carries neither.

batch_size 12 amortises the instructions prefix across up to twelve filings per call, and each call is a process spawn, so the batch size sets how long a run takes; the filings in a call share one context, which the document accepts and states as the cost of the saving.

source.section: Step 3 — Judge the filing against the commitment (LLM)

llm.prompt_instructions:
You are checking one lobbying filing against what the same organisation has said in public.

Return a JSON object with exactly these two fields:

1. "alignment": exactly one of — Contradicts | Matches | Unclear | No commitment given
   - "Contradicts": the filing asks government for the opposite of what the commitment says.
   - "Matches": the filing asks government for what the commitment says.
   - "Unclear": the two texts are about different things, or neither supports nor conflicts with the other.
   - "No commitment given": the commitment line is blank, or reads `nan` or `None` because no commitment was on record for that organisation. Answer this and nothing else in that case — do not judge, and do not supply a commitment yourself.

2. "alignment_note": one plain sentence naming what the organisation said in public and what this filing asks for. Empty string when there is no commitment to compare against.

Judge only the two texts in front of you. Do not use anything you know or believe about the organisation, and never invent, complete or paraphrase a commitment that is not printed here.

stages.description: Put Every Contradiction in Front of a Person
compiler_notes: queue.filter selects only the filings the model called 'Contradicts': those are the only ones the report prints as a finding, so queueing the other three labels would spend a reviewer's attention on rows nothing is claimed about.

The reviewer's label is ADDED as reviewed_alignment; the model's alignment is never overwritten, so the run records both what the model said and what the person decided, and the report can print the second beside the first.

reviewed_alignment is non-nullable: a queued row's reviewer picks one of the four labels, and a row the filter passed over carries the model's label through unchanged, so no filing reaches the report unlabelled.
queue.sort puts the largest reported spend first, so the costliest filing is read while the reviewer is fresh. It orders the review, not the stage's output.

The signature reads every column the reviewer needs on the card: the reviewer sees exactly what the signature reads, and a decision made without the commitment and the ask in front of them would be a decision about the model's label.

source.section: Step 4 — Put every contradiction in front of a person

queue.reviewer_instructions: You are the last reader before this filing is published as a contradiction, and the report will carry your name against it. Read the commitment as said and the ask as filed, and decide from those two texts — the model's label is a suggestion, and agreeing with one you have not checked is how a wrong finding gets published under your name. Keep 'Contradicts' only if this filing asks government for the opposite of what the client promised; if the two are about different things, or the filing asks for what was promised, change the label to the one that fits. Then say in the note which words in the two texts you decided from.

compiler_notes: The document says this is a reading aid, not a verdict — no score, ranking or recommendation column is rendered. A row that contradicts shows the two texts the judgment was made from and adds nothing.

What is printed is reviewed_alignment, the label as the reviewer left it. The model's alignment is read too, but only to say what a reviewer changed it FROM — nothing on this page claims a contradiction the model alone asserted.
A filing published as contradicting a commitment the join never matched stops the step: the page must not show a contradiction it cannot print both sides of.
A filing with no commitment on record says so in its own cell rather than rendering an empty one, so the join's non-matches are visible on the page and not just in lineage.
The page's markup lives in this step, beside the code that fills it, so a reviewer reads both together rather than chasing a file the workflow does not carry.
This stage writes the HTML to disk and returns a file-path pointer rather than embedding the markup inline, which is practical at scale.

corner_cases.expected: its cell prints the label alone — the model's, carried through — with no reviewer against it
